entries.name: Albania

officialName.note: Wikipedia infobox (Republika e Shqipërisë) and the constitution's wording 'Republic of Albania'.

capital.note: Constitution Article 14(6): 'The capital city of the Republic of Albania is Tirana.'

population.note: UN WPP 2024 revision, 1 July 2024 medium variant: 2,791,765 (read via Worldometers, which states it reproduces the 2024 Revision; the UN data-portal API requires a token). Rounded to 3 significant figures. The Wikipedia UN list showed 2,811,655 for 2023, consistent with the trend.

areaSqKm.note: Total area including inland water. Verified in the Wikipedia area list (rank 140): total 28,748 km2 = land 27,400 km2 + water 330 km2 (about 1.1% water).

languages.note: Constitution Article 14(1): 'The official language in the Republic of Albania is Albanian.'

currency.note: Symbol L, ISO ALL, issued by the Bank of Albania.

landmarks.note: Albania's three UNESCO World Heritage sites are Butrint and the historic centres of Berat and Gjirokastër; the castle is the best-known sight in Gjirokastër.

funFact.value: Albania's communist government dotted the country with small concrete bunkers from 1967 to 1986, an average of about 5.7 for every square kilometer.
funFact.note: 148 characters. The Wikipedia article gives construction years 1967-1986 and 5.7 bunkers per km2; its total count is inconsistent between sources, so the fact deliberately avoids a total.

driveSide.note: Verified: Wikipedia traffic table row 'RHT 1926'. Agrees with the seed.

flag.text: Albania's flag is plain red with a black two-headed eagle. The eagle comes from the seal of Skanderbeg's Kastrioti family, who fought the Ottomans in the 1400s; two-headed eagles were also a Byzantine imperial symbol. Ismail Qemali raised this flag when he declared independence on 28 November 1912. The 2002 flag law only describes the design; red is often said to mean bravery and blood shed for freedom, but no law says so.

reasons.feature: Black two-headed eagle in the center
reasons.why: Derived from the coat of arms of the Kastrioti family of Skanderbeg (black double-headed eagle on red, used in his 1443-1479 resistance to the Ottomans); Wikipedia says he adopted the similar Eastern Roman (Byzantine) imperial flag, and the emblem became the symbol of the Albanians.

reasons.feature: Red background
reasons.why: Neither the constitution (Art. 14: 'red with a two-headed black eagle in the centre') nor Law 8926 of 2002 gives the color a meaning; the Wikipedia article states 'the red stands for bravery, strength, valour and bloodshed' without citing a legal source, so the app text presents it as 'often said'.

reasons.feature: Adoption: raised 28 November 1912; current design set by law in 2002
reasons.why: Verified on Wikipedia: Ismail Qemali raised the flag at the declaration of independence in Vlorë on 28 November 1912; a communist gold star added on 10 January 1946 was removed on 7 April 1992; Law Nr. 8926 of 22 July 2002 standardized the present flag.

entries.remainingDoubts: Population comes from Worldometers' reproduction of WPP 2024 (2,791,765), not directly from the UN portal. The bunker total is disputed between sources, so the fun fact gives only the density figure from Wikipedia. The Albanian text of Law 8926 was not opened; the flag description relies on Wikipedia's account and the constitution. Wikipedia states the red-color meaning as fact but without a legal citation, so it is kept hedged. Wikipedia also notes there is no surviving evidence of the exact appearance of the flag raised in 1912.

entries.name: Andorra

officialName.note: Wikipedia infobox.

capital.note: Wikipedia infobox; at 1,023 m it is described as the highest capital city in Europe.

population.note: UN WPP 2024 revision, 1 July 2024 medium variant: 81,938 (read via Worldometers, which states it reproduces the 2024 Revision). Rounded to 3 significant figures. The Wikipedia UN list showed 80,856 for 2023. Andorra's own statistics office reports a higher resident figure (about 90,000), but the rule asks for WPP.

areaSqKm.note: Total area 468 km2 from the Wikipedia infobox. The Wikipedia area list was fetched twice but the returned excerpt was cut off before Andorra's row, so the list figure itself was not seen; Andorra has negligible inland water, so land and total area coincide.

languages.note: 'The sole official language is Catalan' (Constitution Art. 2); Spanish, Portuguese and French are also used but are not official.

currency.note: Euro under a monetary agreement with the EU; Andorra is not an EU member.

value: Casa de la Vall (Andorra la Vella)
Church of Sant Joan de Caselles
landmarks.note: All three are named in the Andorra article: Casa de la Vall (historic parliament seat since 1702), the Madriu-Perafita-Claror Valley (UNESCO World Heritage Site) and the 11th-century Romanesque church of Sant Joan de Caselles. The church's parish (Canillo) was not confirmed in an opened page, so no place qualifier is given.

funFact.value: Andorra has two heads of state at once, known as co-princes: the Catholic Bishop of Urgell in Spain and the President of France.
funFact.note: 128 characters. Wikipedia: 'headed by two co-princes: the Bishop of Urgell in Catalonia, Spain, and the president of France.' The institution is constitutional and stable.

driveSide.note: Verified: Wikipedia traffic table row 'RHT 1724'; infobox 'Driving side: right'. Agrees with the seed.

flag.text: Andorra's flag has blue, yellow and red upright bands with the coat of arms in the middle. Adopted in 1866, it is often said to mix the blue and red of France with the yellow and red of Catalonia and Spain. On the shield, a bishop's hat and staff stand for the Bishop of Urgell, the red stripes for Foix and Catalonia, and the two cows for Béarn, all old powers over Andorra. The motto means united virtue is stronger; a 1996 law fixed the design.

reasons.feature: Three upright bands of blue, yellow and red
reasons.why: Wikipedia: the blue and red are also found on the French flag, and red and yellow are the colors of Catalonia (and the old County of Foix); no law states a meaning for the colors, so the reading is hedged as 'often said'. The civil flag dates from 1866 and is traditionally attributed to Napoleon III.

reasons.feature: Coat of arms: mitre and crozier, three red stripes, four red stripes, two red cows
reasons.why: The quarters stand for the Bishop of Urgell (mitre and crozier), the Counts of Foix (three red vertical stripes on gold), Catalonia (four red stripes on gold) and the Viscounty of Béarn (two red cows): the co-princes and the historic powers linked to Andorra. The arms are named in Article 2(2) of the 1993 Constitution.

reasons.feature: Motto VIRTUS UNITA FORTIOR under the shield
reasons.why: Latin for 'United virtue is stronger' (also rendered 'strength united is stronger'); reported as introduced with the 1931 redesign of the arms.

reasons.feature: Adoption and legal basis
reasons.why: Design in use since 1866; standardized after the 1993 Constitution and UN admission; the Law on the use of State symbols (approved 20 June 1996, promulgated 10 July 1996) defines the traditional flag and arms in its annex.

entries.remainingDoubts: The 1996 symbols law was identified from the WIPO Lex search result and its summary, not read in full, so the exact wording of its annex is unverified. The 1866 date and Napoleon III attribution are traditional per Wikipedia. The row for Andorra in the Wikipedia area list was not visible in either fetched excerpt; 468 km2 comes from the country infobox. Population is from Worldometers' reproduction of WPP 2024 (81,938).

entries.name: Bosnia and Herzegovina

officialName.note: The state's full name is simply 'Bosnia and Herzegovina' (the 'Republic of' form used in 1992-1995 was dropped under the Dayton constitution).

capital.note: Wikipedia infobox: capital and largest city.

population.note: UN WPP 2024 revision, 1 July 2024 medium variant: 3,164,253 (read via Worldometers, which states it reproduces the 2024 Revision). Rounded to 3 significant figures. The Wikipedia UN list showed 3,185,073 for 2023.

areaSqKm.note: Total area including inland water. Verified in the Wikipedia area list (rank 125): total 51,209 km2 = land 51,200 km2 + water 10 km2.

languages.note: The state constitution names no official language (Wikipedia infobox 'Official languages: None'); Bosnian, Croatian and Serbian are the three recognised languages of the state and the official languages of its entities, and are the languages used officially in practice.

currency.note: Symbol KM, ISO BAM; fixed at 1 EUR = 1.95583 BAM.

landmarks.note: Stari Most (Old Bridge, commissioned 1557, destroyed 1993, rebuilt 2004, UNESCO), Sarajevo's old bazaar Baščaršija, and the Kravica (Kravice) waterfalls on the Trebižat river.

funFact.value: Bosnia and Herzegovina reaches the Adriatic Sea along a coastline of only about 20 kilometers, and its capital Sarajevo hosted the 1984 Winter Olympics.
funFact.note: 152 characters. Both facts from the Wikipedia country article (20 km coastline; 1984 Winter Olympics in Sarajevo).

driveSide.note: Seed says Right. The Wikipedia traffic table was fetched again for this check, but the returned excerpt was again truncated before the Bosnia row, so the value is not confirmed from an opened page; no opened source disagreed, and all neighbouring countries (Croatia, Serbia, Montenegro) drive on the right.

flag.text: Bosnia's parliament could not agree on a flag, so on 4 February 1998 High Representative Carlos Westendorp imposed this design by Mladen Kolobarić; its blue and yellow match the Council of Europe flag. The triangle's three corners are usually read as the three main peoples, Bosniaks, Croats and Serbs, and its shape as the country's outline. The white stars are usually read as Europe, running off the edges to suggest an endless row.

reasons.feature: Adoption: imposed 4 February 1998 by the High Representative
reasons.why: After the Parliamentary Assembly failed to adopt a flag law on 3 February 1998, High Representative Carlos Westendorp announced and imposed the Law on the Flag on 4 February 1998; the design was by Mladen Kolobarić, chosen from alternatives prepared by a commission set up on 12 January 1998.

reasons.feature: Blue background and yellow triangle colors
reasons.why: Westendorp's decision states that 'the blue and yellow colours used in the flag have been amended and shall be the blue and yellow of the flag of the Council of Europe'; the blue background is thus deliberately evocative of the European flag.

reasons.feature: Yellow triangle (three corners, shape)
reasons.why: Commonly explained, including in press reports at the time, as the three constituent peoples (Bosniaks, Croats and Serbs) and the approximate shape of the country's territory; the flag law itself (Article 3) only describes the geometry and gives no meaning, so this is hedged as 'usually read as'.

reasons.feature: Row of white stars cut off at the top and bottom
reasons.why: Described as representing Europe, with the stars 'meant to be infinite in number' and therefore continuing off the top and bottom edges; not stated in the law.

reasons.feature: White, blue and yellow palette overall
reasons.why: Wikipedia notes these are colors often associated with neutrality and peace and traditionally with Bosnian culture; this is a popular reading, not part of the law.

entries.remainingDoubts: Drive side (Right) still not confirmed from an opened page: two fetches of the Wikipedia traffic table were both truncated before the Bosnia row and the infobox excerpt omitted the line; it matches the seed and all neighbours. The symbolic meanings of the triangle and stars are reported by Wikipedia and 1998 press summaries but do not appear in the OHR decision or the flag law text; the designer's name comes from Wikipedia only. Population is from Worldometers' reproduction of WPP 2024 (3,164,253). The 'official languages' answer follows the pragmatic reading (three recognised languages) since the state constitution names none.

entries.name: Croatia

officialName.note: Wikipedia infobox: Republic of Croatia (Republika Hrvatska).

capital.note: Single capital, no accents in the Wikipedia title.

quizCapital.note: Single capital; identical to the capital string.

population.note: UN WPP 2024 revision mid-2024 estimate 3,875,325 (read via Worldometers' table of WPP 2024 data; the Wikipedia UN list only showed the 2023 column, 3,896,023). Rounded to 3 significant figures: 3,880,000. Not re-fetched from the UN portal in the review pass.

areaSqKm.note: Per Wikipedia's list by area: total 56,594 km2 = 55,974 land + 620 inland water. The Croatia article infobox shows a slightly different national figure (56,561); the list value is used as the rules require.

languages.note: Croatian is the sole official language per the Wikipedia infobox (constitution Art. 12). Minority languages have only local official status and are excluded.

currency.note: Croatia adopted the euro on 1 January 2023, replacing the kuna.

landmarks.note: Well-known UNESCO-listed sights; chosen from general knowledge, not individually verified.

funFact.value: The necktie traces back to the cravat, a scarf worn by Croatian soldiers in France in the 1600s that Parisians soon copied.
funFact.note: Wikipedia: Croatian mercenaries in French service wore the neckcloth; in 1660 a regiment of Croats arrived in France and their costume was imitated. 123 characters.

driveSide.note: Wikipedia table lists Croatia as right-hand traffic (switched in 1918). Matches seed leftHand=false.

flag.text: Croatia's flag was set by law on 21 December 1990, just before independence from Yugoslavia. The red, white and blue bands date from 1848 and are the Pan-Slavic colors; the law gives them no meaning. The red and white checkerboard is Croatia's old coat of arms, recorded on a seal in 1527. Five small shields above it show historical arms, left to right: the oldest known Croatian arms, Dubrovnik, Dalmatia, Istria and Slavonia.

reasons.feature: Three horizontal bands of red, white and blue
reasons.why: Used as the Croatian flag since 1848; they are the Pan-Slavic colors shared with several Slavic nations (Flag of Croatia article, confirmed in review). The 1990 law (Narodne Novine 55/90) prescribes the three equal bands but assigns no meaning to the colors.

reasons.feature: Red and white checkerboard shield in the center
reasons.why: The traditional Croatian coat of arms: first attested as a decoration in 1495 and officially on the seal of the 1527 Cetingrad Charter (per the Coat of arms of Croatia article). The Flag of Croatia article confirms the checkerboard was added to the flag from 1939; the 1990 law fixed its position with the crown over the red band and the base over the blue band.

reasons.feature: Crown of five small shields above the checkerboard
reasons.why: The 1990 law (Art. 7) lists them left to right: the oldest known Croatian arms (gold star over a silver crescent on blue; Wikipedia labels this one Central Croatia), the Republic of Dubrovnik (two red stripes on blue), Dalmatia (three crowned golden leopard heads), Istria (golden goat with red horns and hooves) and Slavonia (a marten between two silver stripes for the Sava and Drava rivers, with a star). Order confirmed in review against the Flag of Croatia article.

reasons.feature: Adoption and designer
reasons.why: Officially adopted on 21 December 1990 (confirmed in review), months before the 1991 declaration of independence; the design is credited to painter and graphic artist Miroslav Šutej.

reasons.feature: Meaning of the colors
reasons.why: Neither the law nor the Flag of Croatia article gives an official meaning for red, white and blue beyond their Pan-Slavic and historical origin, so the text says no meaning is given.

entries.remainingDoubts: Area: Wikipedia's list gives 56,594 km2 while the Croatia article infobox gives 56,561; the list figure was used per the rules. Population came from Worldometers' table of WPP 2024 data rather than the UN portal itself. Landmarks were not individually verified. The 1495 and 1527 checkerboard dates rest on the Coat of arms of Croatia article and were not re-verified in the review pass; the Flag of Croatia article confirmed 1848, 1939, 21 December 1990, the five-shield order and Šutej. Flag text is 428 characters, inside the 450 limit but above the 420 aim.

population.note: Per ownerRules, Kosovo Agency of Statistics press release 'Population Estimate, 2024': 1,585,590 resident inhabitants. Rounded to 3 significant figures: 1,590,000. The 2024 census counted 1,585,566; UN WPP figures for Kosovo are higher and were not used.

areaSqKm.note: Wikipedia list by area (unranked row, CIA World Factbook source): 10,887 km2 total, all land, no inland water listed.

languages.note: Albanian and Serbian are the official languages per the Wikipedia infobox (Constitution Art. 5). Turkish, Bosnian and Romani have official status only at municipal level and are excluded.

currency.note: Kosovo uses the euro unilaterally; it is not a eurozone member.

landmarks.note: Well-known sights chosen from general knowledge; not individually verified.

funFact.value: Kosovo declared independence from Serbia in 2008; about half of the world's countries recognize it, and Serbia does not.
funFact.note: Agreed status sentence per ownerRules, verbatim (120 characters). Wikipedia: declaration 17 February 2008; recognized by about half of UN member states, consistent with 'about half'.

driveSide.note: Matches seed leftHand=false. The Wikipedia traffic table fetch was truncated before the Kosovo row; a travel-guide search result confirms right-hand traffic, as in all neighboring countries.

flag.text: Kosovo's flag was adopted on 17 February 2008, the day it declared independence from Serbia. It won a design competition held under UN-led talks, whose rules said the flag must show all of Kosovo's peoples and avoid Albanian or Serbian symbols like the double-headed eagle. The gold shape is a map of the country on blue. The six white stars stand for Kosovo's six main communities: Albanians, Serbs, Bosniaks, Turks, Roma and Gorani.

reasons.feature: Gold map of Kosovo on a blue background
reasons.why: The design chosen by the Assembly of Kosovo shows the territory of the country itself; Wikipedia (confirmed in review): the flag is unusual among national flags in using a map, and the flag of Cyprus is the only other to do so.

reasons.feature: Six white stars in an arc
reasons.why: Wikipedia (confirmed in review): the stars symbolize Kosovo's six major ethnic groups: Albanians, Serbs, Bosniaks, Turks, Romani and Gorani. The text uses the common English form 'Roma' for Romani.

reasons.feature: Adoption date and competition
reasons.why: Adopted 17 February 2008, immediately after the declaration of independence (confirmed in review). The international competition drew 993 entries; the Kosovo Symbols Commission selected three designs and the Assembly chose a modified version of the one by Muhamer Ibrahimi. Under the UN-led settlement process, symbols had to reflect Kosovo's multi-ethnic nature, avoiding the Albanian or Serbian double-headed eagles or solely red-and-black or red-blue-white color schemes.

reasons.feature: Meaning of the blue, gold and white colors
reasons.why: No official meaning for the colors is given in the Flag of Kosovo article (confirmed in review), and it does not say the colors were chosen to resemble the EU flag, so the text makes no claim about them.

entries.remainingDoubts: Drive side was not confirmed from the Wikipedia traffic table (fetch truncated); it rests on a travel-guide search result and the seed. The 'Roma' star simplifies Wikipedia's 'Romani'. No official meaning for the colors was found. Flag text is 434 characters. Landmarks not individually verified.

quizCapital.note: Single capital; identical to the capital string.

areaSqKm.note: 316 km2 total for the archipelago (Malta, Gozo, Comino and islets); inland water is negligible. Taken from the Malta article infobox because the list page fetch was truncated before the Malta row.

languages.note: Constitution Art. 5: Maltese is the national language; Maltese and English are official. landmarks.note: Ġgantija verified as a UNESCO site on Gozo; the other two are well-known sights chosen from general knowledge.

funFact.value: The Ġgantija temples on Gozo were built around 3600 BC, making them older than Stonehenge and Egypt's pyramids.
funFact.note: Wikipedia: built around 3600 BC, more than 5,500 years old, predating Stonehenge and the pyramids; UNESCO listed 1980. 111 characters.

driveSide.note: Wikipedia table lists Malta as left-hand traffic (former British colony). Matches seed leftHand=true.

flag.text: Malta's flag is white by the pole and red outside, as its 1964 independence constitution requires. A legend credits Count Roger of Sicily with the colors in 1091, but historians call it a myth; they more likely come from the Knights of St John's white cross on red. The George Cross, edged in red, in the upper left corner was given by King George VI in 1942 for Malta's bravery under heavy bombing in World War II; it joined the flag in 1943.

reasons.feature: Two upright halves, white next to the pole and red on the outer side
reasons.why: Laid down in the Constitution of Malta (Article 3, National Flag) adopted at independence on 21 September 1964; Wikipedia (confirmed in review) states the constitution requires the white side at the pole and the red side on the outer side.

reasons.feature: Origin of the white and red colors
reasons.why: A popular legend says Count Roger I of Sicily gave Malta its colors in 1091 by tearing a piece from his red and white banner; Wikipedia (confirmed in review) says this has been debunked as a 19th-century myth. The more credible origin is the flag of the Knights of St John (Knights of Malta), a white cross on red, who ruled the islands from 1530 to 1798.

reasons.feature: George Cross in the upper left corner, edged in red
reasons.why: King George VI bestowed the George Cross on Malta on 15 April 1942 for the islanders' conduct during the World War II siege and bombing. It was officially added to the flag on 28 December 1943 on a blue square; at independence on 21 September 1964 the blue square was replaced by a thin red edge (all dates confirmed in review). The medal shows St George slaying the dragon and the words For Gallantry, visible in the flag image.

reasons.feature: Meaning of white and red
reasons.why: No official meaning for the colors is given in the constitution or the Flag of Malta article (confirmed in review); only their technical shades are specified.

entries.remainingDoubts: Area 316 km2 comes from the Malta article infobox; the list-by-area page fetch was truncated before Malta. The constitution PDF was opened but only its table of contents was read, so the wording of Article 3 rests on Wikipedia's summary (which confirms white at the pole, red outside and the George Cross edged in red). Inclusion of Maltese Sign Language follows the South Africa model entry but depends on owner policy (2016 Act, not the constitution). Population came from Worldometers' WPP 2024 table rather than the UN portal. Flag text is 443 characters, under the 450 limit but above the 420 aim.

entries.name: Montenegro

officialName.note: The 2007 constitution and the Wikipedia infobox use the plain name Montenegro; there is no longer a 'Republic of' prefix.

capital.note: Constitution Article 5: 'The capital of Montenegro shall be Podgorica. The Old Royal Capital of Montenegro shall be Cetinje.' Cetinje holds a ceremonial title and hosts the president's seat but is not a co-capital, so only Podgorica is given.

population.note: UN WPP 2024 revision, medium variant, 1 July 2024: 638,479 (as republished in Worldometers' yearly table, which cites WPP 2024). Rounded to 3 significant figures. The UN data-portal API itself returned 401, so the figure was not read from population.un.org directly; the Wikipedia UN list (WPP 2024) gives 633,552 for mid-2023, consistent with this value.

areaSqKm.note: Total area from Wikipedia's list (re-checked in review): 13,888 km2 = 13,450 km2 land + 438 km2 inland water (Lake Skadar etc.). The country article infobox says 13,883 km2 and the national statistics office uses 13,812 km2; the list value is used per the field rule.

languages.note: Constitution Article 13: Montenegrin is the official language (Cyrillic and Latin equal); Serbian, Bosnian, Albanian and Croatian 'shall also be in the official use'. Wikipedia labels those four 'recognised national languages'. Only the official language is listed; owner may add the four if 'in official use' should count.

currency.note: Montenegro uses the euro unilaterally; it is not a eurozone member and has no formal agreement with the ECB.

landmarks.note: All three are named as main attractions in the Tourism in Montenegro article: Boka Kotorska with Kotor's UNESCO-listed old town; Durmitor and the Tara canyon (UNESCO-listed national park); Sveti Stefan island hamlet.

funFact.value: The name Montenegro comes from Venetian for Black Mountain, a translation of Crna Gora, named for the dark evergreen forests of Mount Lovćen.
funFact.note: 141 characters. Wikipedia: the English name is a literal translation of a Venetian calque of 'Crna Gora' (Black Mountain), from the appearance of Mount Lovćen covered in dense evergreen forests.

driveSide.note: Seed leftHand=false; worldstandards.eu country table: Montenegro drives on the right. No source disagreed.

flag.text: Adopted in 2004, the flag is based on the royal banner of King Nikola I: red with a gold border and the coat of arms. The two-headed eagle, a symbol of Byzantine origin, was used by the Crnojević rulers in the 1400s and is often read as church and state united. Its crown, scepter and orb copy Russian imperial arms. Prince-Bishop Sava added the lion shield in the 1700s as a sign of church authority. The law gives the colors no meaning.

reasons.feature: Red cloth with a gold border and the coat of arms in the center
reasons.why: Prescribed by the Law on State Symbols and the Day of Statehood (in force 13 July 2004, Article 5: 'red with the coat of arms in the middle and with a golden border') and by Article 4 of the 2007 constitution.

reasons.feature: Overall design (red and gold banner with eagle)
reasons.why: The 2004 flag is based on the old royal banner used under King Nikola I (ruled 1860-1918); red and gold were the colors of the Petrović-Njegoš rulers' flags.

reasons.feature: Golden two-headed eagle
reasons.why: Wikipedia's coat-of-arms article: the two-headed eagle is 'a symbol of Byzantine and ultimately ancient Roman origin', and 'the history of the state coat of arms begins with the Crnojević dynasty in the 15th century'.

reasons.feature: Two heads of the eagle read as church and state
reasons.why: Wikipedia says the double-headed eagle 'symbolizes either the unity of or the close connections between the church and the state' (Montenegro was long ruled by prince-bishops); the 2004 law assigns no such meaning, so this is a traditional reading.

reasons.feature: Crown above the eagle, scepter and orb in its claws
reasons.why: Wikipedia: 'The current layout of the coat of arms of Montenegro was taken from that of the Russian Empire, with which the ruling House of Petrović-Njegoš had close ecclesiastical, dynastic and political ties in the 19th century.' The scepter and orb were added by Prince-Bishop Sava in the 18th century.

reasons.feature: Shield on the eagle's chest with a golden walking lion on blue over green
reasons.why: Per the Wikipedia coat-of-arms article, Prince-Bishop (vladika) Sava Petrović-Njegoš, who ruled in the 18th century, removed the family arms from the eagle's breast, added the scepter and orb, and 'added another symbol retained until present day - a golden lion passant'. The lion 'is as a sign of episcopal authority and could have been conceived of as a metaphor for the Lion of Judah' (the Lion of Judah link is a hypothesis, not an official meaning).

reasons.feature: Red and gold colors
reasons.why: Neither the 2004 law nor the constitution gives any meaning to the colors.

entries.remainingDoubts: Population comes from Worldometers' republication of WPP 2024 (the UN portal API was not accessible), not from the UN site itself. Area: three figures circulate (13,888 list / 13,883 infobox / 13,812 official); the list value was used as instructed and re-confirmed on the Wikipedia list page. Languages: whether the four languages 'in official use' should be listed is an owner decision. Flag: the review corrected the draft, which credited Prince Danilo with adding the lion shield; the Wikipedia coat-of-arms article credits vladika (Prince-Bishop) Sava, who ruled in the 18th century, so the text now says 'Prince-Bishop Sava ... in the 1700s'; the exact year was not given in the fetched passage. Wikipedia names Radoslav Rotković as designer of the 2004 version, which was not independently verified and is not used in the text. The 2004 law text was read via Flags of the World, not the official gazette.

funFact.value: Lake Ohrid, shared with Albania, is one of Europe's oldest and deepest lakes, up to 288 meters deep, and home to more than 200 species found nowhere else.

flag.text: Adopted in 1995, the flag shows a yellow sun with eight widening rays on a red background. Designer Miroslav Grčev's sun is the new sun of liberty named in the national anthem. It replaced a 1992 flag bearing the sixteen-ray Vergina Sun, an ancient Macedonian symbol, after Greece objected and imposed a trade embargo; a 1995 accord ended the flag dispute. Red and yellow continue from earlier flags; the colors have no official meaning.

reasons.feature: Yellow sun with eight widening rays reaching the edges
reasons.why: Adopted on 5 October 1995 from a design by architect Miroslav Grčev; Wikipedia (re-checked in review): the sun 'represents the new sun of Liberty referred to in Denes nad Makedonija', the national anthem, and has 'eight broadening rays extending from the centre to the edge of the field'.

reasons.feature: Why the 1992 Vergina Sun flag was replaced
reasons.why: The 1992-1995 flag bore the sixteen-ray Vergina Sun, found at the ancient Macedonian royal tombs at Aegae in Greece; Greece saw this as a claim on its heritage and 'imposed a year-long economic embargo'; 'the blockade was lifted in October 1995 when an agreement was reached to change the flag' (the Interim Accord of September 1995). The name dispute itself was settled only later, by the 2018 Prespa Agreement.

reasons.feature: Red background with yellow (gold) emblem
reasons.why: Red with a gold emblem continues the color scheme of the earlier flags (the 1946-1992 red flag with a gold star and the 1992 red flag with the gold Vergina Sun).

reasons.feature: Meaning of the colors red and yellow
reasons.why: The Wikipedia flag article (re-checked in review) gives no symbolic meaning for the red and yellow colors; only the sun is explained.

funFact.value: Portugal's border with Spain has barely changed since the Treaty of Alcañices in 1297, which makes it one of Europe's oldest fixed frontiers.
funFact.note: 141 characters. Wikipedia: 'With minor readjustments, Portugal's borders have largely remained the same since the signing of the Treaty of Alcañices... in 1297.' The 'one of Europe's oldest' comparison is a common statement but was not itself quoted in the opened source.

driveSide.note: Seed leftHand=false; worldstandards.eu table says Portugal drives on the right, and Wikipedia notes Portugal switched to right-hand traffic in 1928.

flag.text: After the 1910 revolution ended the monarchy, the flag became law in 1911. Green and red were the republicans' colors, often said to mean hope and blood shed for Portugal. The yellow armillary sphere was King Manuel I's emblem in the Age of Discoveries. The five small blue shields date from the 1100s; the tale of a 1139 battle is a myth. The seven castles on the red border are often tied to the Algarve conquest, but their origin is unclear.

reasons.feature: Green (2/5) and red (3/5) vertical bands
reasons.why: Red and green had been the colors of the Portuguese Republican Party since the failed republican revolt of 31 January 1891; after the republic was proclaimed on 5 October 1910 a commission chose them, the flag was presented on 1 December 1910 and made official by decree on 30 June 1911.

reasons.feature: Official reasoning for the colors
reasons.why: The 1910 commission's report called red 'the battling, warm, virile colour' of conquest and blood, and justified green as the color of the 1891 republican flag that 'sparked the redeeming lightning' of the republic.

reasons.feature: Green as hope, red as the blood of those who died for the nation
reasons.why: This popular reading was promoted in the decades after 1911 to give the colors a patriotic rather than party-political sense; it is not the commission's wording.

reasons.feature: Yellow armillary sphere behind the shield
reasons.why: A navigation instrument that King Manuel I (1495-1521) used as his personal emblem; it recalls the Portuguese voyages of the Age of Discoveries and appeared on ships of that era.

reasons.feature: White shield with five small blue shields each bearing five white dots
reasons.why: The arms of Portugal's first kings from the 12th century. Legend says Afonso Henriques defeated five Moorish kings at Ourique in 1139 and that the dots are Christ's wounds, but Wikipedia calls this 'pure myth': the legend was first written down in 1419 and the number of dots varied for centuries.

reasons.feature: Red border with seven golden castles
reasons.why: Traditionally said to stand for castles taken from the Moors in the Algarve under Afonso III (completed 1249), but the number of castles varied (16, 12, 7, 11) until fixed at seven; another hypothesis links them to the castles of Castile through Afonso III's Castilian mother and wife. No settled meaning exists.

entries.remainingDoubts: Population taken from Worldometers' republication of WPP 2024 rather than the UN portal (API returned 401). Area: list value 92,090 differs from infobox 92,225; the list value was used as instructed and re-confirmed on the list page. Fun fact: the 1297 treaty is verified; the 'one of Europe's oldest frontiers' comparison is widely stated but not quoted from the opened source. Flag: the 1910 commission wording comes from the Wikipedia flag article (which cites the commission report); no Portuguese government page on the flag was opened within the call budget.

landmarks.note: Guaita and Cesta are two of the three towers (Guaita, Cesta, Montale) named in the coat of arms and flag sources opened; the flag article also records the 1829 flag being hoisted at the Guaita. funFact.value: San Marino has two heads of state at once, the Captains Regent, who are elected together and serve for only six months at a time.
funFact.note: Wikipedia: the Grand and General Council 'selects two heads of state, the Captains Regent, every six months ... serve concurrently with equal powers'. 129 characters; the practice dates to the Middle Ages so it is stable.

driveSide.note: Seed leftHand=false → Right. Confirmed via search snippet of the worldstandards list (San Marino not among left-driving countries, drives on the right). The Wikipedia traffic table fetch was truncated before San Marino's row, so that page is cited for general context only. No source disagreed.

flag.text: The white and light blue two-band flag was first recorded in 1829; the colors are often said to mean peace and liberty, but no law says so. The feather-topped towers on three green peaks are the fortresses Guaita, Cesta and Montale on Monte Titano. The crown, added in 1862, means independence, not a king. Oak and laurel are said to show stability and defense of liberty. LIBERTAS, Latin for freedom, is the national motto. Fixed by law in 2011.

reasons.feature: White band over light blue band
reasons.why: Wikipedia's flag article: in 1797 the Supreme Council commissioned a white and blue cockade (under French Revolutionary influence); the first recorded white-and-light-blue two-band flag was hoisted at the Guaita in 1829; the infobox gives 'Early 1800s (standardised on 22 July 2011)'. The exact layout and colors were fixed by the constitutional law of 22 July 2011 on the flag and coat of arms.

reasons.feature: Meaning of white and light blue (peace and liberty)
reasons.why: Wikipedia states the two colors represent peace (white) and liberty (light blue) but does not attribute that meaning to any law; the 2011 law text quoted by FOTW only describes the flag and gives no color meaning, and FOTW says no official meaning is documented. Presented as a popular reading ('often said to').

reasons.feature: Three white towers on three green peaks, each topped by an ostrich feather
reasons.why: The towers are the three citadels Guaita, Cesta and Montale and the hills are the three summits of Monte Titano; the feathers are the towers' weather vanes drawn heraldically. The 2011 law blazons 'three mountains Vert, three towers Argent ... topped by ostrich plumes Argent'.

reasons.feature: Closed crown above the shield
reasons.why: Added by decree of 6 April 1862 (the flag article confirms the 1862 decree standardized the coat of arms); the 2011 law states the arms are 'surmounted by a closed crown, symbol of sovereignty' (independence, not a monarchy).

reasons.feature: Oak (viewer's right) and laurel (viewer's left) branches
reasons.why: Wikipedia's coat of arms article describes them as symbols of the stability of the republic and the defense of liberty; FOTW gives the more generic 'military strength and glory'. No law text giving a meaning was found, so hedged with 'are said to'.

reasons.feature: White scroll reading LIBERTAS
reasons.why: LIBERTAS (Latin for freedom) is the national motto, linked to the republic's long independence and its tradition of sheltering refugees; it possibly derives from the alleged last words of the founder Marinus.

reasons.feature: Adoption / standardization
reasons.why: Wikipedia infobox: adopted early 1800s, standardized by the Law on the flag and coat of arms of 22 July 2011.

entries.remainingDoubts: The 2011 law PDF on consigliograndeegenerale.sm could not be parsed, so the statement that the law gives no color meaning rests on the article quoted by FOTW, FOTW's own remark and Wikipedia's unattributed wording; if the law's preamble does state 'peace and liberty', upgrade that reason from traditional to official. Palazzo Pubblico as a landmark was not verified from an opened page. Area: the list gives 61 km2 while the country infobox gives 61.19 km2; 61.0 used per the list. Population was not re-fetched in the review pass.

funFact.note: Coat of arms article: Grand Prince Stefan Nemanja (r. 1166-1196) was among the first in Serbia to use the symbol, so 'over 800 years ago' stays true. The heavenly/earthly reading is given on the Serbian government's symbols page as 'is said to'; hedged with 'tradition says'. 148 characters.

driveSide.note: Seed leftHand=false → Right. Confirmed via search snippet (driving in Serbia is on the right). The Wikipedia traffic table fetch was truncated before Serbia's row, so that page is cited for context only. No source disagreed.

flag.text: Red, blue and white are the Pan-Slavic colors; Serbia's order dates to 1835. No law gives the colors a meaning; tradition reads red as blood, blue as freedom, white as mother's milk. The white two-headed eagle is a Byzantine symbol of the medieval Nemanjić kings. The cross with four curved marks on its chest is popularly read as Cyrillic S letters: Only unity saves the Serbs. Crown and gold lilies copy the 1882 royal arms. Adopted in 2004.

reasons.feature: Three bands red, blue, white
reasons.why: Pan-Slavic colors shared with Russia and other Slavic nations. Wikipedia: the 1835 Sretenje Constitution named red, white and steel-blue; after Ottoman and Russian objections a December 1835 firman permitted the order red (top), blue, white. The story that Prince Miloš simply turned the Russian white-blue-red flag upside down is marked 'reportedly' in the article, so only the 1835 date is used in the text.

reasons.feature: Meaning of the colors
reasons.why: No official meaning: the flag article gives no symbolic meaning for the colors, only technical specifications. The government's symbols page relays a traditional reading (red = blood shed for the country, blue = freedom, white = nurturing milk) and notes flag experts see only generic meanings.

reasons.feature: White double-headed eagle on red shield, set toward the left
reasons.why: Byzantine symbol used in Serbia since the 11th century, adopted as the arms of the Nemanjić dynasty (Stefan Nemanja, r. 1166-1196) and formally by Stefan Lazarević in 1402; the current arms are based on the 1882 arms of the Kingdom of Serbia. The flag article confirms the lesser coat of arms is centered vertically and shifted toward the flagpole by one-seventh of the flag's length. The government page says one head is said to face the heavenly kingdom and the other the earthly one.

reasons.feature: Serbian cross with four firesteels (curved marks) on the eagle's chest
reasons.why: Resembles the late Byzantine imperial emblem with four firesteels; the flag article notes Emperor Stefan Dušan (1346) adopted the Byzantine style of a white cross with four firesteels on red. The reading of the firesteels as four Cyrillic S letters for 'Only unity saves the Serbs' is a modern folk etymology, so it is given as 'popularly read'.

reasons.feature: Golden crown with cross above the shield
reasons.why: Part of the royal arms of the Kingdom of Serbia enacted in 1882 (the flag article: a Serbian eagle on a red shield crowned with a golden crown), on which the current arms are based; the law describes it as golden with pearls, sapphires and rubies but assigns no meaning.

reasons.feature: Two golden fleurs-de-lis (lilies) under the eagle's claws
reasons.why: Present in the 1882 royal arms that the current design copies; the flag article does not mention them and no meaning or origin is given in the sources opened.

reasons.feature: Adoption
reasons.why: Flag article infobox: state flag adopted 2004, standardized 2010. Body: the National Assembly's 2004 recommendation reintroduced the flag with the coat of arms, the 2009 Law on National Symbols legally sanctioned it, and a 2010 standardization fixed the color values and redrew the arms.

entries.remainingDoubts: Area: the Wikipedia list value is 88,499 km2 (includes Kosovo); 77,589 km2 (excluding Kosovo, Serbia article infobox) was chosen for consistency with the owner's population rule; the CIA alternative is 77,474 km2. Owner should confirm which convention the app uses. Whether the crown depicts a specific dynasty's crown could not be confirmed, so the text only ties it to the 1882 arms. Landmarks were not verified from opened pages. The reversed-Russian-flag story is marked 'reportedly' by Wikipedia, so it is kept out of the text. Population was not re-fetched in the review pass.

flag.text: White, blue and red are Pan-Slavic colors, first raised in Ljubljana in 1848 and taken from the coat of arms of Carniola. No law gives them a meaning. Adopted in June 1991 at independence from Yugoslavia, the flag swapped a red star for a shield by Marko Pogačnik: the white peak is Triglav, Slovenia's highest mountain; two wavy lines are the sea and rivers; three gold stars come from the Counts of Celje; the red edge has no given meaning.

reasons.feature: Three bands white, blue, red
reasons.why: Considered Pan-Slavic colors (shared with Russia, Serbia, Slovakia etc.), but Wikipedia states they actually come from the medieval coat of arms of the Duchy of Carniola; the white-blue-red flag was first raised by Lovro Toman in Ljubljana on 7 April 1848 in answer to a German flag over Ljubljana Castle (re-checked in this pass).

reasons.feature: Meaning of the colors
reasons.why: Neither the flag article (re-checked: no stated symbolic meaning) nor the government's national-symbols page gives any meaning for white, blue or red; only the historical and Pan-Slavic associations.

reasons.feature: Coat of arms in the upper left, half in white and half in blue
reasons.why: Placement fixed by the constitution and the 1994 Act Regulating the Coat-of-Arms, Flag and Anthem; the flag article and government page state it sits in the upper left centered on the white and blue bands. It replaced the red star of the Socialist Republic of Slovenia's flag (1945-1991).

reasons.feature: White mountain (Triglav) on blue shield
reasons.why: Mount Triglav, Slovenia's highest peak, drawn in white; the arms were designed by Marko Pogačnik, who won a 1991 tender, and adopted on 24 June 1991. The designer additionally read the silhouette as 'the male principle' (his own interpretation, not in law).

reasons.feature: Two wavy blue lines under the mountain
reasons.why: The government page says they symbolize the sea and rivers; the flag article says the Adriatic Sea and local rivers; the coat of arms article adds the Triglav Lakes Valley and the Slovene coast.

reasons.feature: Three golden six-pointed stars in a point-down triangle

funFact.value: Vatican City is the world's smallest independent state by both area and population, and it lies entirely inside the city of Rome.
funFact.note: 129 characters. Wikipedia lead (confirmed this session): 'the smallest country in the world both by area and by population' and 'an enclave within the city of Rome, Italy'. Stable for the foreseeable future.

driveSide.note: Seed leftHand=false, so Right; consistent with Italy, which completely surrounds the state. A grep of the Vatican City article this session found no 'Driving side' row in its infobox, so this is not independently confirmed from an opened source; no source disagreed.

flag.text: Adopted in 1929, when the Lateran Treaty created the state. Yellow and white date from 1808, when Pope Pius VII had papal guards swap red for white to set them apart from Napoleon's troops; they also match the gold and silver of the keys. The crossed keys recall the keys of heaven promised to Saint Peter in the Bible and stand for the pope's authority. A red cord ties them; no meaning is given. The triple crown above is the papal tiara.

reasons.feature: Two upright halves, yellow next to the pole and white outside, square shape
reasons.why: Prescribed when the Lateran Treaty of 7 June 1929 created Vatican City State: Article 19 of the 1929 Fundamental Law, restated in Article 20 of the 2000 law and Article 23 (with Attachment A) of the 2023 Fundamental Law, which describe a yellow half at the pole and a white half carrying the tiara with the keys. The law shows a 1:1 (square) flag, one of only two square national flags with Switzerland; in 2010 the Apostolic Nunciature to Germany stated the flag does not have to be square. Confirmed on the Wikipedia flag article this session.

reasons.feature: Yellow and white colors
reasons.why: Before 1808 the Papal States used a yellow and red flag (the traditional colors of the Roman Senate and people). In 1808 Pope Pius VII ordered the Noble Guard and other papal troops to replace red with white so they could be told apart from troops that had been incorporated into Napoleon's army. Yellow and white were kept for the new state in 1929. Confirmed on the Wikipedia flag article this session.

reasons.feature: Yellow and white matching the gold and silver keys
reasons.why: Wikipedia's flag article states that the yellow and white merchant flag adopted by the Papal States on 17 September 1825 'took its colours from the materials of the two keys (yellow for gold, white for silver)'. No law gives the colors a meaning, so the text says only that they 'also match' the keys rather than claiming an official symbolism.

reasons.feature: Crossed gold and silver keys
reasons.why: The keys of heaven, which the Gospel of Matthew (16:19) says Jesus promised to Saint Peter, are the long-standing emblem of papal authority used in the arms of the Holy See and Vatican City; the law specifies one gold and one silver key crossed. The popular reading of gold = power in heaven and silver = power on earth is only traditional and, for length, was left out of the text.

reasons.feature: Red cord tying the keys
reasons.why: The law's model shows the keys bound by a red cord with tassels, but neither the law nor the sources opened give it a meaning, so the text says no meaning is given. (A separate, widespread error colors the inner lining of the tiara red instead of white; it spread from a Wikimedia Commons image used in 2006-07 and 2017-22, and Attachment A of the 2023 Fundamental Law shows the correct white lining.)

reasons.feature: Papal tiara (triple crown) with white ribbons above the keys
reasons.why: Required by the Fundamental Law ('the tiara with the keys', part of the emblem of the Holy See); it is the three-tiered crown historically worn by popes and marks the emblem as that of the papal state. The sources opened give no official meaning for the three tiers, so the text calls it simply the papal tiara, a triple crown.

entries.remainingDoubts: (1) Area: Wikipedia's area list gives 0.44 km2 and calls it the official figure (itself tagged 'dubious' on Wikipedia), while the Vatican City article infobox gives 0.49 km2 (De Agostini 1945-46 correction); I followed the list as instructed, but the maintainer may prefer 0.49. (2) Drive side: taken from the seed and Italy's practice; the Vatican City infobox has no driving-side row, so it is not confirmed from an opened source. (3) The official law text (2023 Fundamental Law, Art. 23 and Attachment A) was not opened directly; the draft reported vaticanstate.va returning 404, so it is cited via Wikipedia's flag article and the EWTN article. (4) The gold = heaven / silver = earth reading of the keys is traditional and was dropped from the flag text for length; the red cord is left without a meaning because none is documented. (5) Population 496 is the UN WPP 2024 mid-2024 figure as ownerRules require (taken from Worldometers' WPP-2024 table since the UN data portal was not opened), far below the Vatican's own resident count of about 882.

flag.text: Red-white-red is one of Europe's oldest flag designs: the three bands appear on a seal of Austria's ruling Babenberg dukes in 1230. A popular legend says Duke Leopold V's white tunic was soaked with blood at the siege of Acre in 1191 except under his belt, but historians call this a later story, not fact. The republic adopted the flag in 1918 and again in 1945, and a 1984 law fixes it. No official meaning is given to the colors.

reasons.feature: Three horizontal bands red, white, red
reasons.why: Taken from the arms of the Babenberg dukes of Austria (a silver band on a red shield); the design is first documented on a seal attached to a deed of 30 November 1230 confirming the privileges of Lilienfeld Abbey.

reasons.feature: Red-white-red origin story (Leopold V at Acre)
reasons.why: Tradition says Duke Leopold V's white surcoat was drenched in blood at the Siege of Acre (1189-1191) except under his belt. First written down around 1260; Wikipedia and historians describe it as a legend, so the entry hedges it.

reasons.feature: Adoption and legal basis
reasons.why: Adopted by German Austria in 1918 after Austria-Hungary dissolved, re-adopted on 1 May 1945, and set in § 3 of the Wappengesetz 1984 (BGBl. Nr. 159/1984): 'Die Farben der Republik Österreich sind rot-weiß-rot' and the flag has three equal horizontal stripes, the middle white, the upper and lower red.

reasons.feature: Meaning of the colors
reasons.why: Neither the Wappengesetz nor the flag's Wikipedia article gives any symbolic meaning to red and white beyond their heraldic origin, so the entry says no official meaning is given.

flag.text: The flag comes from the orange, white and blue colors of William of Orange, leader of the Dutch revolt against Spain in the 1570s, worn by his soldiers and flown on his ships. By about 1660 orange had given way to red: some say the dye faded, others that it marked a political move away from the House of Orange. Queen Wilhelmina fixed red, white and blue by decree on 19 February 1937. No official meaning is given to the colors.

reasons.feature: Red, white and blue as the legal colors

reasons.feature: Meaning of the colors

flag.text: At the Battle of Laupen in 1339, Swiss soldiers sewed a white cross onto their clothing to tell friend from foe, and it became the shared sign of the old Swiss Confederacy. Why the background is red is debated: some say the blood of Christ, others the flag of Bern. The design was set for Swiss troops in 1841 and written into the constitution of 1848. The square shape comes from old war banners. The colors have no official meaning.

reasons.feature: White cross
reasons.why: First documented at the Battle of Laupen in 1339, where it was sewn onto soldiers' clothing as two strips of cloth to mark them out from their enemies; it became the common battlefield sign of the Old Swiss Confederacy. Confirmed this run on both the Wikipedia flag article and the Swiss government's aboutswitzerland page.

reasons.feature: Red background
reasons.why: Origin is debated. The Swiss government's aboutswitzerland page says some historians think the red refers to the blood of Christ while others suspect it comes from the Bernese flag of the time; a link to the old red flag of Schwyz is also often suggested. The Wikipedia flag article gives no settled explanation.

reasons.feature: Adoption as national flag
reasons.why: The Tagsatzung (federal diet) prescribed the unified white cross on red for the infantry of the cantons in 1841, following a resolution of 1840; the 1848 federal constitution prescribed it as the flag of the federal troops (the government page says it was definitively enshrined in the constitution in 1848); the Federal Council published the official details and proportions in 1889.

reasons.feature: Square shape
reasons.why: Inherited from the late medieval and early modern war flags carried by Swiss infantry regiments, rather than the rectangular shape most national flags take from the maritime tradition; both sources say that apart from Vatican City it is the world's only square national flag.

reasons.feature: Fixed proportions and shade of red
reasons.why: The Coat of Arms Protection Act in force since 2017 defines the flag as a square with a centered white cross whose arms are one sixth longer than they are wide, and fixes the red as Pantone 485C (RGB 255-0-0, hex FF0000); the one-sixth rule dates from the Federal Council's 1889 definition.

reasons.feature: Meaning of the colors
reasons.why: No official meaning is assigned to red or white; the government page offers only competing historical theories for the red, and the Wikipedia article records no official symbolism for the colors.

entries.remainingDoubts: Population is the WPP 2024 mid-2024 figure (8,921,981) as reproduced by Worldometer, not read from the UN data portal directly; the Wikipedia UN list only shows 2022 and 2023 columns. flag.text: The design dates from 1951, when Belarus was a Soviet republic. After a 1995 vote the hammer, sickle and star were removed, leaving a wide red band over a narrow green one. No law gives the colors a meaning; the president has described red as freedom and sacrifice and green as life, and green is often linked to the forests. The red-on-white pattern by the flagpole copies a design woven in 1917 by Matrona Markevich for a traditional cloth.

reasons.feature: Wide red band over a narrower green band (two thirds / one third)
reasons.why: The layout is inherited from the flag of the Byelorussian Soviet Socialist Republic adopted by decree on 25 December 1951. It was brought back by the referendum of 14 May 1995 and fixed by Presidential Decree No. 214 of 7 June 1995; the official presidential page describes the proportions but gives no meaning.

reasons.feature: No hammer, sickle or star
reasons.why: The Soviet emblems that sat on the red band of the 1951 flag were dropped when the design was revived in 1995, after four years of the white-red-white flag used 1991-1995.

reasons.feature: Red color
reasons.why: No law or official page fixes a meaning (confirmed on the Wikipedia flag article). President Lukashenko has described red as freedom and the sacrifice of the nation's forefathers; in the 1951 Soviet design it stood for communism. Presented in the text as a statement, not a legal meaning.

reasons.feature: Green color
reasons.why: No legal meaning. The president has called it life; it is popularly linked to the country's fields and forests (Britannica).

reasons.feature: Red-on-white ornamental stripe beside the flagpole

flag.text: Adopted in 1879, soon after Russia helped free Bulgaria from Ottoman rule, the flag copies the Pan-Slavic white, blue and red of Russia and other Slavic nations but swaps blue for green. The constitution describes it only as white, green and red bands and gives the colors no meaning. They are often said to stand for peace, the fertile land and the courage of those who fought for freedom. A communist emblem added in 1947 was removed in 1990.

reasons.feature: Three horizontal bands, white over green over red
reasons.why: Set out in Article 23 of the 1879 Tarnovo Constitution after the Russo-Turkish War of 1877-78 (constitution adopted 16 April 1879), and today by Article 166 of the 1991 Constitution and the 1998 Law on the State Seal and National Flag, which describe only the colors and order.

reasons.feature: White and red shared with Russia; green in place of blue (Pan-Slavic colors)
reasons.why: The design was modeled on the Russian white-blue-red flag out of Slavic solidarity with the liberators of 1878, with green substituted for blue (Britannica; the Wikipedia flag article does not discuss this link).

reasons.feature: Meaning of white, green and red
reasons.why: Neither the constitution nor the flag law assigns meanings (confirmed on the Wikipedia flag article, which lists no official symbolism). Britannica records the popular reading: white for peace, love and freedom; green for the country's agricultural wealth; red for the independence struggle and military courage. Hedged in the text as often said.

reasons.feature: Plain bands with no emblem
reasons.why: The communist state arms were added to the upper left of the white band under the Dimitrov Constitution of 1947 (modified in 1971); the plain three-band flag was restored on 27 November 1990 and confirmed by the 1991 Constitution.

entries.remainingDoubts: Reviewer changed the emblem date from 1948 to 1947 on the strength of the Wikipedia flag article (Dimitrov Constitution, 1947); some sources give 1948, so the exact year is slightly uncertain. The Pan-Slavic/Russian link rests on Britannica, not the Wikipedia flag page. Area differs between Wikipedia's list (110,879) and the country infobox (110,994); the list value is used. flag.text: White and red come from the coat of arms of Bohemia, a white lion on a red shield, and were Czechoslovakia's colors from 1918. Because that two-band flag looked like Poland's, Jaroslav Kursa added a blue triangle on the flagpole side in 1920; blue is a color of Moravia and Slovakia. When Czechoslovakia split in 1993 the Czech Republic kept the flag. No law gives the colors a meaning; they are often read as Bohemia, Moravia and Slovakia.

reasons.feature: White upper band and red lower band
reasons.why: Taken from the medieval coat of arms of Bohemia, a white double-tailed lion on a red shield; the new state of Czechoslovakia used a plain white-over-red flag from 1918.

reasons.feature: Blue triangle on the flagpole side
reasons.why: Added in 1920 because the white-red flag was almost identical to Poland's flag of 1919 (only the proportions differed). The design by Interior Ministry archivist Jaroslav Kursa was approved by the National Assembly on 30 March 1920; blue referenced Slovakia's white-blue-red colors and the blue shield of Moravia's arms.

reasons.feature: Same flag as former Czechoslovakia
reasons.why: Although the 1992 dissolution agreement contained a clause forbidding either successor state from using Czechoslovak state symbols, the Czech Republic adopted the 1920 flag as its own in 1993 (Act on State Symbols, in force from 1 January 1993).

reasons.feature: Meaning of white, red and blue
reasons.why: The 1993 Czech law names only the colors white, red and blue and gives them no meaning (confirmed on the Wikipedia flag article). A common reading has white for Bohemia (and the sky), red for Moravia (and blood shed for freedom) and blue for Slovakia, now sometimes said to mean impartiality and sovereignty. Hedged as often read.

entries.remainingDoubts: Reviewer re-opened the Wikipedia flag article and the flag image: Kursa, 30 March 1920, the Poland similarity, the dissolution-agreement clause and the absence of legal color meanings are confirmed; all three visible features (blue triangle, white band, red band) are covered. flag.text: Hungary's three bands of red, white and green were first made the national flag by law during the 1848 revolution against Habsburg rule. The colors come from the medieval coat of arms, with its red and white stripes and a white cross on green hills. The plain flag used today dates from 1957, when a communist emblem was removed from the center. The 2011 constitution says red stands for strength, white for faithfulness and green for hope.

reasons.feature: Red, white and green colors
reasons.why: Taken from the Hungarian coat of arms, essentially unchanged since the mid-15th century: red and silver (white) stripes on one half, a silver cross on green hills on the other. From the 15th century the three colors appear together as twisted silk cords on the seals of official documents, and they were displayed at the 1790 coronation of Leopold II.

reasons.feature: Three horizontal bands as national flag
reasons.why: Adopted during the 1848 revolution; Act XXI of 1848 for the first time mandated the red-white-green flag as a national symbol. Wikipedia says the stripes are horizontal rather than vertical to prevent confusion with the Italian flag (even though the Hungarian banner in that form predates the Italian one by at least 7 years).

reasons.feature: Plain bands with no emblem
reasons.why: The current plain version has been the official flag since 23 May 1957, after the communist-era (Rákosi) coat of arms was removed following the 1956 uprising; reaffirmed 19 June 1990.

reasons.feature: Color meanings (strength, fidelity, hope)
reasons.why: The Fundamental Law, in force since 1 January 2012 (Article I of the Foundation chapter), states the red, white and green bands are the symbols of strength (erő), fidelity (hűség) and hope (remény) respectively. An older folk reading (red for blood spilled for the fatherland, white for freedom, green for the pastures) is traditional only and is not used in the text.

entries.remainingDoubts: WPP 2024 mid-2024 value was read from Worldometers' mirror of the UN series because the UN portal API returned 401; not re-checked against the UN site. The Fundamental Law wording on strength/fidelity/hope was confirmed via the Flag of Hungary article, but the article number (Article I of the Foundation chapter) was not confirmed from the law text itself this session. flag.text: Moldova's flag uses the blue, yellow and red of neighboring Romania, with which it shares a language and history. It was adopted in 1990 as Moldova moved toward independence from the Soviet Union. In the center an eagle holds a cross in its beak, an olive branch read as peace and a scepter for power; its shield shows an aurochs head, emblem of medieval Moldavia, with a star, a rose and a crescent. No official meaning is given for the colors.

reasons.feature: Three upright bands of blue, yellow and red
reasons.why: Wikipedia: the flag is based on the flag of Romania, reflecting the two countries' national and cultural affinity (shared language; most of today's Moldova was part of Romania between the world wars).

reasons.feature: Adoption in 1990
reasons.why: The Supreme Soviet of the Moldavian SSR adopted the three-band flag on 27 April 1990 (now Flag Day); the version with the coat of arms, dated 6 November 1990 in the Wikipedia infobox, followed once the arms were approved. Law No. 217 of 17 September 2010 (in force 26 November 2010) fixed the exact shades and made the reverse a mirror of the front.

reasons.feature: Eagle holding a cross, olive branch and scepter
reasons.why: The dark golden eagle comes from the interwar coat of arms of the Kingdom of Romania; it holds an Orthodox cross in its beak and, in its claws, an olive branch (in place of a sword) and a scepter. Wikipedia states the olive branch symbolizes peace; the scepter is usually read as power or sovereignty. These readings are not shown to be stated in the law, so the text hedges with 'read as'.

reasons.feature: Shield with aurochs head, star, rose and crescent
reasons.why: The shield carries the traditional symbols of Moldova: an aurochs head with an eight-pointed star between its horns, a rose on one side and a crescent on the other, all in gold, the historic emblem of the medieval Principality of Moldavia; the arms were designed by Gheorghe Vrabie and adopted in 1990.

reasons.feature: Meaning of blue, yellow and red
reasons.why: Wikipedia's flag article gives no official symbolic meaning for the individual colors; the 2010 law only names the shades (Berlin blue, chrome yellow, vermilion red).

entries.remainingDoubts: Currency written with ISO code MDL because the symbol is not standardized in the sources read (Leu/Lei vs L). Area and UN population include Transnistria, which Moldova does not control. Two 1990 adoption dates exist (27 April 1990 for the plain three bands by the Supreme Soviet; 6 November 1990 in the Wikipedia infobox for the flag with arms); the text says only '1990'. Olive branch = peace is stated in Wikipedia; scepter = power/sovereignty was not confirmed from the law text, hence the hedged wording. WPP mid-2024 value read from Worldometers' mirror of the UN series.

flag.text: Poland's flag is white above red. The colors come from the national coat of arms, a white eagle on a red shield, carried by Polish kings since the Middle Ages. In 1831, during an uprising against Russian rule, the parliament declared white and red the national colors, and the flag was adopted by law in 1919, after Poland regained independence. White goes on top because the eagle ranks above its shield. The law gives the colors no meaning.

reasons.feature: White and red colors
reasons.why: Heraldic origin: the White Eagle of Poland (and the white knight of Lithuania) on a red shield; a red banner with the White Eagle was the Banner of the Kingdom of Poland from the reign of Ladislaus the Short (1320-1333).

reasons.feature: White and red declared national colors
reasons.why: On 7 February 1831, during the November Uprising against Russian rule, the Sejm adopted white and red, the tinctures of the Polish and Lithuanian arms, as the national cockade.

reasons.feature: Two horizontal bands, adopted 1919
reasons.why: The Sejm established the white-and-red flag on 1 August 1919 after independence in 1918; the 1980 Coat of Arms Act fixed exact color values and the 1997 Constitution (Art. 28) names white and red as the national colors.

reasons.feature: White on top
reasons.why: In Polish heraldry the color of the emblem (the White Eagle) is placed in the more honorable upper position above the color of its shield (red).

reasons.feature: Meaning of the colors
reasons.why: Neither the 1997 Constitution nor the 1980 Act assigns symbolic meanings; the Wikipedia article gives only the heraldic origin, so no meaning is stated.

entries.remainingDoubts: Area 312,685 re-confirmed from the Wikipedia list (Poland article gives 312,696). The variant flag with the eagle in the white band (used abroad and at sea) is not mentioned in the text for length. WPP mid-2024 value read from Worldometers' mirror of the UN series; Poland's flag claims (1831, 1919, Art. 28) were not re-fetched in the review pass and rest on the draft's reading of the Flag of Poland article.

flag.text: Three upright bands of blue, yellow and red. The colors were first flown together in Wallachia in 1834, and in 1848 revolutionaries made blue-yellow-red a national flag, linked at the time to liberty, justice and brotherhood; the upright layout dates from 1867. The constitution and the flag law only name the colors and give them no official meaning. In 1989 protesters cut the communist emblem out of the center, and the plain flag returned.

reasons.feature: Blue, yellow and red bands
reasons.why: The three colors appeared together on a Wallachian flag design submitted for Ottoman approval in 1834 (the first documented use of the three colors together), and the provisional government's Decree No. 1 of June 1848 made a blue-yellow-red flag national, with the motto Justice, Fraternity; historians read the colors of that period as liberty (blue), justice (yellow) and fraternity (red). The 1866 constitution fixed the colors.

reasons.feature: Vertical (upright) arrangement of the bands
reasons.why: The 1848 flag had horizontal stripes; the Assembly of Deputies decided on 26 March 1867 that the colors be placed vertically, blue next to the pole, yellow in the middle, red outermost. The 1991 constitution (Article 12) keeps that order.

reasons.feature: Meaning of the colors today
reasons.why: Article 12 of the constitution and Law 75/1994 only describe the colors, their order and proportions (2:3); no official meaning is assigned. Popular readings (sky, wheat fields, blood of those who died for freedom) circulate but are not in the law.

reasons.feature: Plain flag with no emblem in the center
reasons.why: From 20 December 1989 protesters in Timișoara waved flags with the communist coat of arms cut out of the middle (the flag with the hole); the plain three-band flag was officially restored on 27 December 1989 and confirmed by Law 75/1994, whose 2023 revision added exact color specifications (Pantone 280c, 116c, 186c).

entries.remainingDoubts: Law 75/1994 itself was not opened; its content (description and dimensions only, 2023 shade update) is taken from the Wikipedia flag article. The 1848 reading as liberty-justice-fraternity is a historians' interpretation reported by Wikipedia; the decree's own motto was Justice, Fraternity, so the text says 'linked at the time to'. Population comes from worldometers' reproduction of WPP 2024, not the UN portal; the Wikipedia UN list opened in review shows only 2022-2023 columns. Area: list says 238,398, country article 238,397. Bran Castle was not verified in an opened source. The near-identical flag of Chad is omitted from the text for length.

flag.text: Peter the Great made white, blue and red bands the flag of Russian merchant ships in 1705; the layout is often said to copy the Dutch flag he admired. It became the national flag in 1896, was banned after 1917 and returned in 1991 as Soviet rule ended. The 2000 flag law gives the colors no meaning, though many say white is nobility, blue loyalty and red courage. Other Slavic nations copied these Pan-Slavic colors in 1848.

reasons.feature: Three horizontal bands of white, blue and red
reasons.why: White-blue-red flags are attested on Peter the Great's ships in the 1690s (the exact first date is contested), and his decree of 20/31 January 1705 made the white-blue-red flag the commercial maritime flag. An imperial order of 29 April 1896, before the coronation of Nicholas II, designated it the sole national flag; the Bolsheviks banned it after the 1917 October Revolution; it was restored on 22 August 1991; the Federal Constitutional Law of 25 December 2000 fixes it as three equal horizontal stripes, white, blue, red, ratio 2:3.

reasons.feature: Dutch-style three-band layout
reasons.why: Two accounts connect the design to the flag of the Dutch Republic: a Dutch-built frigate Peter ordered in 1693 arrived in 1694 flying the Dutch red-white-blue, and Peter saw Dutch ships at Arkhangelsk; FOTW notes the design was borrowed while the colors were already traditional in Russia. Wikipedia presents the Dutch link as a widely repeated account, not a documented decree, so it is hedged as 'often said to'.

reasons.feature: Meaning of the colors
reasons.why: The 2000 Federal Constitutional Law only describes the stripes; FOTW states plainly that officially the colors mean nothing and that interpretations were invented long after adoption.

reasons.feature: Popular reading of the colors
reasons.why: The most common reading is white for nobility and frankness, blue for faithfulness, honesty, impeccability and chastity, red for courage, generosity and love; another links the three colors to the historic regions of White, Little and Great Russia. These are traditions, not law.

reasons.feature: Shared Pan-Slavic colors
reasons.why: Wikipedia: the colors later inspired the selection of the Pan-Slavic colors at the Prague Slavic Congress of 1848, which influenced the flags of other Slavic nations such as Slovakia, Slovenia and Serbia.

entries.remainingDoubts: Population from worldometers' reproduction of WPP 2024 rather than the UN portal (the Wikipedia UN list opened in review shows only 2022-2023); Crimea treatment in the UN figure not checked. The first date of the flag is contested (1693/1694 ship at Arkhangelsk vs the 1705 decree); the text uses the documented 1705 decree. Sources differ on when the flag became official on land: Wikipedia says the 29 April 1896 imperial order, FOTW mentions 1883; the text uses 1896. The automated summary of the Wikipedia flag article in review described the nobility/faithfulness/courage reading as 'official', which conflicts with FOTW and with the 2000 law's text as previously read; the entry keeps 'no official meaning' and treats that reading as traditional. constitution.ru returned 503 earlier, so the constitution was read via constituteproject.org. Red Square and the Hermitage not verified in an opened page.

flag.text: White, blue and red bands with the coat of arms near the pole. Slovaks adopted these Pan-Slavic colors in 1848. The arms were added in 1992 so the flag would not match Russia's. On its red shield a white double cross stands on three blue hills: the hills are traditionally read as the Tatra, Fatra and Matra mountains, and the cross is a Christian symbol often linked to the missionaries Cyril and Methodius. The law gives the colors no meaning.

reasons.feature: Three horizontal bands of white, blue and red
reasons.why: Slovaks first used white, blue and red in the revolutionary year 1848; they are the Pan-Slavic colors that Slavic nations took from Russia's flag at the 1848 Prague Slavic Congress. The plain three-band flag was readopted on 1 March 1990.

reasons.feature: Coat of arms placed toward the pole
reasons.why: Added when the constitution took effect on 3 September 1992 specifically to distinguish the flag from Russia's identical white-blue-red bands; Article 9 of the constitution places the state emblem in the left half of the flag, and Act 63/1993 details the design.

reasons.feature: Three blue hills
reasons.why: Traditionally read as the mountain ranges Tatra, Fatra and Matra, an interpretation dating to the 15th-16th century for the arms of the mountainous north of the Kingdom of Hungary; the hills were enlarged in the 1990 design to stress them as a national symbol. Not defined in law.

reasons.feature: White double cross on a red shield
reasons.why: A Christian symbol that came to the region from Byzantium through King Bela III of Hungary (12th century); popular tradition links it to the missionaries Cyril and Methodius, though historians note no evidence for that link. Hedged as 'often linked to'.

reasons.feature: Meaning of the colors
reasons.why: The constitution (Articles 8-9) and Act 63/1993 describe the flag and arms only; no meaning is assigned to white, blue or red.

Act 63/1993 was not opened; its role is taken from the Wikipedia flag and coat-of-arms articles. languages.note: Danish is the de facto national language; no constitution or law designates an official language. German is recognized as a minority language in Southern Jutland and Danish Sign Language is recognized, but neither is official nationwide.

currency.note: ISO code DKK. Denmark joined the EC in 1973 but kept its own currency. Format matches the repository's existing 'Norwegian Krone (kr)' and 'Swedish Krona (kr)' entries.
