funFact.value: Denmark proper is the Jutland peninsula plus over 400 named islands; the Kingdom also includes the Faroe Islands and Greenland in the North Atlantic.
funFact.note: 155 characters. Wikipedia: metropolitan Denmark comprises the Jutland peninsula and an archipelago of 406 islands; the Kingdom also includes the autonomous Faroe Islands and Greenland. Hand edit after the workflow: Denmark has about 1,400 islands in all, 443 of them named, so the fact says named islands.

driveSide.note: Seed leftHand=false. The fetched excerpt of the traffic article did not print Denmark's table row explicitly, but it treats Denmark as right-hand traffic like the rest of continental Europe; no source found disagrees.

flag.text: Denmark's flag is called the Dannebrog. A legend from the 1500s says it fell from the sky to help the Danish king win a battle near today's Tallinn in 1219, but historians treat this as a story. Danish kings flew red banners with a white Christian cross from the 1300s; the other Nordic countries later copied the off-center cross. No law gives the colors a meaning; red is often tied to battle and the white cross to faith.

reasons.feature: White cross on a red background
reasons.why: Danish kings used a red banner with a white cross from at least the 14th century; the cross is the Christian cross of the crusading era, a design also seen on other war banners of the time. Earliest firm evidence: the Gelre Armorial (c. 1340-1370) and royal seals from 1356.

reasons.feature: Legend of the flag falling from the sky in 1219
reasons.why: A tradition first recorded in the 16th century (by the friar Petrus Olai) says the flag fell from heaven during Valdemar II's battle at Lyndanisse (Lindanise, near today's Tallinn) on 15 June 1219. Historians treat it as legend; contemporary evidence appears only a century or more later.

reasons.feature: Off-center cross shared with the other Nordic flags
reasons.why: The Danish design was later adopted by Sweden, Norway, Finland, Iceland and the Faroe Islands, so the Nordic cross family traces back to the Dannebrog.

reasons.feature: Meaning of red and white
reasons.why: No law or official statement gives the colors a meaning. Britannica offers the traditional reading that the red field suggests battle and the white cross the holy cause fought for.

reasons.feature: Name Dannebrog and official status
reasons.why: Britannica renders the name as 'Cloth of the Danes'; Wikipedia says it probably means 'red cloth' (Frisian dan = red, Old Norse brok = cloth). Proportions were regulated in 1748, it became an army regimental flag in 1785, and it is listed by Guinness as the oldest continuously used national flag (since 1625).

entries.remainingDoubts: Population 2024 value comes from Worldometers' reproduction of WPP 2024 rather than the UN portal directly; the Wikipedia UN list re-checked in review still shows only 2022 and 2023 columns (2023 matches). Area differs between Wikipedia's list (42,947) and the Denmark article (43,094); the list value was used as instructed. Denmark has no single flag law, so 'no law gives the colors a meaning' rests on Wikipedia and Britannica, not on a primary text. The etymology of Dannebrog is disputed between sources, so it was left out of the flag text. Driving side was not printed in the fetched traffic-article excerpt. The Flag of Denmark article was not re-opened in the review pass (call budget), so the Gelre Armorial, 1356 seal, 1748, 1785 and 1625 details stand on the draft's reading.

driveSide.note: Seed leftHand=false; Wikipedia table lists Estonia as RHT.

flag.text: Estonia's flag has three equal bands of blue, black and white, colors chosen by the Estonian Students' Society in 1881 under Russian rule. They became the national flag in 1918; banned under Soviet rule from 1940, the flag flew again over Tallinn in 1989 and was restored by law in 1990. No law gives a meaning, but a popular reading from the poet Martin Lipp makes blue the sky, black the soil and the hard past, and white purity and hope.

reasons.feature: Three horizontal bands of blue, black and white
reasons.why: The Estonian Students' Society (Vironia), founded in 1881 while Estonia was in the Russian Empire, adopted blue, black and white as its colors; its first flag was made in spring 1884 and consecrated at Otepää on 4 June 1884. The colors spread as a symbol of the Estonian nation. Confirmed in review against the Flag of Estonia article.

reasons.feature: Meaning of blue, black and white
reasons.why: The Estonian Flag Act specifies design and shades but assigns no meaning (confirmed in review: the article says the Act sets only color codes and dimensions). The common reading, from Martin Lipp's lyrics set to music in 1922, is blue for the sky over Estonians, black for attachment to the soil of the homeland (and, in wider tradition, the dark fate of past centuries), and white for purity, hard work and commitment (Britannica words it as sky, soil and the aspiration toward freedom).

reasons.feature: Adoption as national flag
reasons.why: The Provisional Government declared it the national flag on 21 November 1918; parliament confirmed it by law on 16 July 1922. After Soviet occupation banned it in 1940 (display remained a punishable crime), it replaced the Soviet flag on Tallinn's Pikk Hermann tower on 24 February 1989 and was formally re-adopted on 7 August 1990. All dates confirmed in review against the Flag of Estonia article.

entries.remainingDoubts: Population 2024 value comes from Worldometers' reproduction of WPP 2024 rather than the UN portal directly (2023 value cross-checks against Wikipedia's UN list). The Constitution (Articles 6 and 7) and the Flag Act were not read directly (Riigi Teataja returned no text; guessed Government Office and Visit Estonia URLs returned 404), so 'no law gives a meaning' rests on the Wikipedia flag article, which was re-read in review and states it explicitly. Britannica dates the first adoption to 24 February 1918 and re-adoption to 8 May 1990, while Wikipedia gives 21 November 1918 and 7 August 1990; the text avoids the disputed days. Lipp's 'hard past' reading of black is the wider tradition rather than Lipp's exact wording ('attachment to the soil'). Euro adoption year (2011) not verified in session.

Re-checked in review: Wikipedia's UN list (WPP 2024) prints 2022 and 2023 only; its 2023 value 5,601,185 matches Worldometers' 2023 row.

areaSqKm.note: Wikipedia area list total: land 303,815 plus 34,330 km2 of inland water; includes the autonomous Åland Islands.

languages.note: Section 17 of the Constitution: 'The national languages of Finland are Finnish and Swedish.' Sámi, Romani and sign languages have protected status but are not national languages. currency.note: ISO code EUR; Wikipedia gives euro adoption as 1999 (cash from 2002).

landmarks.note: All three are named in Wikipedia's Tourism in Finland article; Suomenlinna sea fortress is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

funFact.value: Finland is nicknamed the land of a thousand lakes, but it actually has more than 180,000 of them, set among vast northern forests.
funFact.note: 130 characters. Wikipedia: over 180,000 recorded lakes; the land is predominantly covered by boreal forest.

driveSide.note: Seed leftHand=false; Wikipedia: Finland, formerly part of left-driving Sweden, switched to right-hand traffic in 1858 by Russian decree.

flag.text: Finland's flag is a blue cross on white, in the off-center style that began in Denmark and is shared by all Nordic countries. The writer Zachris Topelius proposed blue and white in the early 1860s, and a Helsinki yacht club had flown a blue cross since 1861. After independence from Russia, it became the national flag by law in 1918. No law explains the colors; blue is traditionally said to be the lakes and sky, white the winter snow.

reasons.feature: Off-center cross
reasons.why: The Nordic cross layout comes from the shared tradition begun by Denmark's Dannebrog (the Flag of Denmark article lists Finland among the countries that adopted the Danish design; the Flag of Finland article speaks of the shared Nordic tradition). In Finland it was first used by the Helsinki yacht club Nyländska Jaktklubben, founded in 1861, whose flag had a blue cross on white with provincial arms; confirmed in review.

reasons.feature: Blue and white colors
reasons.why: The author Zachris Topelius proposed blue and white as Finland's colors (Britannica: summer 1862; Wikipedia: 'about 1860'), and they won popular support. After independence a competition and debate chose them over a red and yellow design with the lion of the coat of arms; Eero Snellman and Bruno Tuukkanen specified the final form. The text was changed in review to 'early 1860s' to cover both datings.

reasons.feature: Meaning of blue (lakes, sky) and white (snow)
reasons.why: Blue is said to represent the country's thousands of lakes and the sky, and white the snow that covers the land in winter; both sources present this as popular interpretation ('is said to'), and the flag law defines only the design, not a meaning. Confirmed in review against the Flag of Finland article.

reasons.feature: Adoption in 1918
reasons.why: The blue cross flag was adopted on 28 May 1918 per Wikipedia (Britannica gives 29 May 1918, the date the Senate endorsed the flag act), shortly after independence from Russia was declared on 6 December 1917. Wikipedia does not name the adopting body, so the text was changed in review from 'parliament made it' to 'it became the national flag by law'. Its Finnish name is siniristilippu, the blue cross flag.

entries.remainingDoubts: Population 2024 value comes from Worldometers' reproduction of WPP 2024 rather than the UN portal directly (2023 value cross-checks against Wikipedia's UN list). The current Act on the Flag of Finland (380/1978) was not read: the Finlex page returned only navigation and the Ministry of the Interior and Foreign Affairs pages returned 404/403, so 'no law explains the colors' rests on the Wikipedia and Britannica flag articles. The Constitution's Section 17 wording was seen in a search snippet, not an opened page. Sources differ on the exact 1918 adoption date (28 vs 29 May) and on which body adopted it; the text gives only the year and says 'by law'. Topelius's proposal is dated 1862 by Britannica and 'about 1860' by Wikipedia; the text says 'early 1860s'.

currency.note: ISO code ISK, symbol kr.

funFact.value: Iceland's parliament, the Althing, first met in 930 at Þingvellir, which makes it one of the oldest parliaments in the world.
funFact.note: Wikipedia: the Althing was established in 930 at Þingvellir and is one of the world's oldest functioning legislative assemblies. 124 characters.

driveSide.note: Matches the seed. Iceland switched from left to right in May 1968 (H-dagurinn).

flag.text: The off-center cross is shared by the Nordic flags and began with Denmark, which once ruled Iceland. Icelanders first flew a white cross on blue, but the Danish king wanted it to look less like other flags, so a red cross was set inside the white one. Approved in 1915, it became the national flag in 1918. A 1944 law calls the colors sky blue, snow white and fiery red, often said to stand for mountains and sea, snow and ice, and volcanic fire.

reasons.feature: Off-center cross (Nordic cross)
reasons.why: The cross layout is the common Nordic design that began with Denmark's flag; Denmark ruled Iceland until the 20th century, and the design also signaled Scandinavian solidarity.

reasons.feature: Blue background with white cross
reasons.why: Comes from the earlier unofficial Icelandic flag Hvítbláinn (a white cross on blue) flown by independence supporters around 1900; the Wikipedia flag article confirms the blue-and-white forerunner but does not give its proposal date, so no year is stated.

reasons.feature: Red cross inside the white cross
reasons.why: Added so the Danish king would approve the flag: the plain white-on-blue was judged too similar to existing flags (often said to be the Greek flag) and the red brought in Denmark's colors. King Christian X approved the design by royal decree on 19 June 1915; it became the national flag on 1 December 1918 when Iceland became a sovereign kingdom.

reasons.feature: Colors: sky blue, snow white, fiery red
reasons.why: Law No. 34 of 17 June 1944, passed when Iceland became a republic, describes the flag as sky-blue with a snow-white cross and a fiery-red cross inside the white cross, and fixes the cross widths (white 2/9, red 1/9 of the flag's height). Wikipedia notes the blue was classed as ultramarine between 1918 and 1944.

reasons.feature: Landscape reading of the colors
reasons.why: Wikipedia: the colors are commonly interpreted as representing the landscape, red for volcanic fire, white for ice and snow, and blue for the mountains and surrounding sea; this is a widely repeated interpretation rather than a meaning written into the law.

entries.remainingDoubts: The official government.is flag page (English text of Act 34/1944) returned HTTP 402 through the proxy, so the law's wording is taken from the Wikipedia article's quotation of it (confirmed on this pass). The exact reason the Danish king rejected the white-on-blue flag could not be confirmed from the Wikipedia flag article on this pass (Britannica says it needed to differ from existing flags and include Danish colors; the Greek-flag similarity is a common account), so the text hedges to 'look less like other flags'. The draft's claims that the 1944 law fixed a darker blue and that blue-white matched the falcon coat of arms were not supported by the Wikipedia flag article and were removed. Population comes from Worldometer's reproduction of WPP 2024 rather than the UN site itself.

currency.note: Eurozone member.

funFact.value: Newgrange, a stone tomb in County Meath built around 3100 BC, is older than Stonehenge, and the winter solstice sunrise lights up its inner chamber.
funFact.note: Wikipedia: built c. 3100 BC, about 500 years older than the current Stonehenge and the Great Pyramid; on the winter solstice the rising sun shines along the passage into the chamber. 148 characters.

driveSide.note: Matches the seed; infobox drives_on = left; one of four European countries with left-hand traffic.

flag.text: Thomas Francis Meagher presented the three-band flag in 1848, inspired by the French flag. Officially, green stands for the older Gaelic and Catholic tradition and orange for the Protestant followers of William of Orange; the white between them, Meagher said, means a lasting truce between the two. It flew over Dublin's General Post Office in the 1916 Easter Rising, and the 1937 Constitution names it the national flag.

reasons.feature: Three upright bands influenced by the French flag
reasons.why: Thomas Francis Meagher of the Young Ireland movement presented the green-white-orange flag in 1848, the year of European revolutions, after the Young Irelanders visited France; the design was influenced by France's three-band flag, and the first Irish tricolour had appeared in 1830 as a gift at a meeting celebrating that year's French revolution.

reasons.feature: Green band
reasons.why: Department of the Taoiseach guidance, as quoted by Wikipedia, says the green symbolizes Roman Catholics (Britannica likewise links it to the Catholic majority and the older Gaelic tradition).

reasons.feature: Orange band
reasons.why: The same official guidance says orange represents the minority Protestants who were supporters of William of Orange; Britannica notes it is often wrongly described as yellow or gold.

reasons.feature: White band in the middle
reasons.why: Meagher said in 1848 that the white in the centre signifies a lasting truce between the Orange and the Green; official guidance says it signifies a lasting peace and hope for union between Protestants and Catholics in Ireland.

reasons.feature: Status as national flag
reasons.why: Raised over the General Post Office in Dublin during the 1916 Easter Rising, adopted by the Irish Free State in 1922, and given constitutional status in 1937 by Article 7: the national flag is the tricolour of green, white and orange.

entries.remainingDoubts: The Department of the Taoiseach's National Flag page (gov.ie) and the Irish Statute Book constitution text both returned 403 through the proxy, so the official color meanings and Article 7 wording are taken from the Wikipedia flag article's quotations of them and from Britannica. On this pass the Wikipedia quotation of the government guidance gave green as symbolizing Roman Catholics; the draft's 'older Gaelic tradition' wording could not be confirmed and was removed from the official-basis reason. Wikipedia describes the French flag as an influence rather than a direct model, so the text says 'inspired by'. officialName is given as Ireland (constitutional name and UN listing) rather than Republic of Ireland; the editor may prefer the descriptive form for display.

flag.text: A chronicle says that around 1279 Latvian warriors from Cēsis carried a red flag with a white stripe, and legend tells of a wounded leader wrapped in a white sheet that his blood stained at both edges. Latvian patriots revived the colors in the 1800s, and Latvia adopted the flag on 15 June 1921. Banned in Soviet times, it returned in 1990. The law fixes the carmine shade and a narrow white band but gives the colors no official meaning.

reasons.feature: Red-white-red bands
reasons.why: The Livonian Rhymed Chronicle records a battle around 1279 involving Latgalian warriors from Cēsis (Wenden) who carried a red flag with a white stripe; this is the documented origin of the colors.

reasons.feature: White stripe between red (legend of the sheet)
reasons.why: A popular account says a mortally wounded Latgalian chief was wrapped in a white sheet; the part he lay on stayed white while the two edges were colored by his blood, and his warriors then used the sheet as a flag. This is folklore attached to the chronicle entry, not a documented event.

reasons.feature: Adoption and revival dates
reasons.why: Latvian nationalists began using the colors again in the 19th century; a first modern design was made in 1916 by Marianna Strautmane from a sketch by Jānis Lapiņš, and the artist Ansis Cīrulis designed the accepted version in May 1917. The Constitutional Assembly affirmed the flag by decree on 15 June 1921. It could not be used under Soviet occupation (1940-41 and 1944-91) and was restored as the national flag on 15 February 1990, before independence was regained in 1991.

reasons.feature: Dark carmine shade and 2:1:2 proportions
reasons.why: Latvian law defines the flag as carmine red with a white horizontal stripe, with the bands in 2:1:2 proportion (red bands twice the width of the white) and an overall height-to-width ratio of 1:2; the statute assigns no symbolic meaning to the colors.

reasons.feature: Meaning of the colors
reasons.why: No official meaning is given in the flag law; the red is sometimes described as the readiness of Latvians to give the blood from their hearts for freedom, but this is a popular reading only.

entries.remainingDoubts: The Law on the National Flag of Latvia on likumi.lv (two URLs), the President's state-symbols page and latvia.eu all returned 404 through the proxy, so the law's content (carmine shade, 2:1:2 proportions, no stated color meaning) rests on the Wikipedia flag article, which was re-read on this pass. The draft's specific claims of an 1870s student revival and a 27 February 1990 restoration were not supported by the article: it says only that nationalists revived the colors in the 19th century and gives 15 February 1990 for the restoration, so the text and reasons now use those. The drive side came back as left in one earlier fetched summary, contrary to the seed; see the driveSide note.

funFact.value: France's national geographic institute calculated in 1989 that the geographic center of Europe lies in Lithuania, north of Vilnius.
funFact.note: 131 characters. Verified: the Wikipedia Lithuania article states that after a 1989 re-estimation of the continent's boundaries, Jean-George Affholder of the Institut Geographique National determined the geographic centre of Europe to be in Lithuania at 54°54′N 25°19′E (Purnuskes), which is north of Vilnius. The exact distance (about 26 km) is not stated in the sentence, so the fact says only north of Vilnius.

flag.text: In 1917 a conference in Vilnius chose the colors. Red and green flags in the hall looked gloomy, so Tadas Daugirdas suggested adding yellow for the rising sun. The flag was adopted in 1918, banned under Soviet rule and restored in 1988. The flag law gives the colors no meaning, but yellow is often said to mean the sun and prosperity, green forests, freedom and hope, and red the blood and courage of those who died for Lithuania.

reasons.feature: Three equal horizontal bands, yellow over green over red
reasons.why: The color scheme emerged at the Vilnius Conference of 1917; a commission of Jonas Basanavicius, Antanas Zmuidzinavicius and Tadas Daugirdas finalized the design and submitted its protocol to the Council of Lithuania on 19 April 1918, and the Council accepted it; the 1922 constitution then adopted the flag still in use. The 1991 Law on the National Flag and Other Flags (No I-1497), Article 2, defines the flag as three equal horizontal colored stripes with yellow above, green in the middle and red below.

reasons.feature: Yellow band added between red and green
reasons.why: At the 1917 conference the hall was decorated with red and green flags, which delegates found too dark and gloomy; Tadas Daugirdas proposed inserting a narrow strip of yellow to symbolize the rising sun between the red (clouds lit up by the morning sun) and the green (fields and forests).

reasons.feature: Meaning of yellow, green and red
reasons.why: The Law on the National Flag and Other Flags (checked in the Seimas English translation) assigns no meaning to the colors; Article 2 describes only their arrangement. The popular explanation, repeated by Wikipedia, is that yellow stands for the sun and prosperity, green for forests, the countryside, liberty and hope, and red for the blood and bravery of those who died for Lithuania; the text therefore hedges it with often said to.

reasons.feature: Ban and restoration; current proportions
reasons.why: Use of the flag was prohibited and prosecuted under Soviet rule; it was re-adopted on 18 November 1988, before the 11 March 1990 declaration of independence. Law No I-1497 of 26 June 1991 re-enacted it, and the 8 July 2004 amendment (Law No IX-2331) changed the ratio from 1:2 to 3:5 (Article 3 now gives 3:5) and made the historical red Vytis banner the separate state flag.

criticApplied.value: Bosnia's parliament could not agree on a flag, so on 4 February 1998 High Representative Carlos Westendorp imposed this design by Mladen Kolobarić; its blue and yellow match the Council of Europe flag. The triangle's three corners are usually read as the three main peoples, Bosniaks, Croats and Serbs, and its shape as the country's outline. The white stars are usually read as Europe, running off the edges to suggest an endless row.
criticApplied.reason: Inconsistent hedging inside one text: the triangle reading is hedged ('usually read as') but the stars reading ('stand for Europe', 'to suggest an endless row') is stated as fact, although the entry's own reason labels it traditional and says it is not in the flag law or the OHR decision. 435 characters.

criticApplied.value: Adopted in 1879, soon after Russia helped free Bulgaria from Ottoman rule, the flag copies the Pan-Slavic white, blue and red of Russia and other Slavic nations but swaps blue for green. The constitution describes it only as white, green and red bands and gives the colors no meaning. They are often said to stand for peace, the fertile land and the courage of those who fought for freedom. A communist emblem added in 1947 was removed in 1990.
criticApplied.reason: Shared-motif consistency: Croatia, Serbia, Slovenia, Slovakia and Russia all name the Pan-Slavic colors in one clause; Bulgaria described the same origin without naming it. Only the label is added; nothing else changes. 444 characters.

criticApplied.value: The red, white and light blue bands probably come from the old coat of arms of Luxembourg's rulers: a red lion on white and blue stripes. The colors were first flown around 1830, and the three-band layout was fixed in 1845. The blue is kept a light sky blue to tell the flag apart from the Dutch one. A 1972 law made the flag official and a 1993 regulation set its exact shades. No official meaning is given to the colors.
criticApplied.reason: 'Laws of 1972 and 1993' is inaccurate: the Wikipedia flag article (opened in this pass) gives the Loi du 23 juin 1972 sur les emblemes nationaux as the law and the Reglement Grand-Ducal of 27 July 1993 as a regulation that defined the colors (Pantone, RGB, CMYK). The entry's own remainingDoubts flagged this. 422 characters.

Consistency: San Marino lists 'Light Blue' while Luxembourg lists plain 'Blue', yet Luxembourg's own flag text calls the band 'light sky blue' and the Wikipedia article describes it as light blue (Pantone 299C, bright blue in contrast to the Dutch flag). Treat both light-blue flags the same way.

criticApplied.value: The design dates from 1951, when Belarus was a Soviet republic. After a 1995 vote the hammer, sickle and star were removed, leaving a wide red band over a narrow green one. No law gives the colors a meaning; the president has described red as freedom and sacrifice and green as life, and green is often linked to the forests. The red-on-white pattern by the flagpole copies a design woven in 1917 by Matrona Markevich for a traditional cloth.
criticApplied.reason: Readability for a 10-year-old: 'the president has called red freedom and sacrifice and green life' is a garden-path sentence. Same facts and sources, only the verb and 'as' are changed. 442 characters.

criticApplied.value: Andorra's flag has blue, yellow and red upright bands with the coat of arms in the middle. Adopted in 1866, it is often said to mix the blue and red of France with the yellow and red of Catalonia and Spain. On the shield, a bishop's hat and staff stand for the Bishop of Urgell, the red stripes for Foix and Catalonia, and the two cows for Béarn, all old powers over Andorra. The motto means united virtue is stronger; a 1996 law fixed the design.
criticApplied.reason: 'all old rulers here' uses a deictic 'here' that has no referent inside a catalog entry and reads oddly in an app; 'all old powers over Andorra' says the same thing explicitly. 447 characters, no other change.
